newsitem.title: JAPAN: Dollar jumps on G7 meeting, higher U.S. rate hopes.
newsitem.headline: Dollar jumps on G7 meeting, higher U.S. rate hopes.

text.p: The dollar jumped to its highest level in more than 2-1/2 years on Monday against the Japanese yen following a harmonious meeting of the G7 nations and an expectation that U.S. interest rates have nowhere to go but up.
The dollar hit 111.22 yen in afternoon trading, its highest since trading at 111.75 yen on January 25, 1994.

It was a bullish response to the weekend meeting of the Group of Seven nations in which the finance ministers and central bank chiefs of the major industrialised nations said they were happy with current exchange rates.
Traders took the statement as a sign that the governments are happy to see the dollar continue to rise.

They also said the dollar was being helped by the expectation of higher U.S. interest rates. Even though the policy-making body of the U.S. Federal Reserve decided at its meeting last week to keep rates steady, analysts say a rate rise is inevitable given the strength of the U.S. economy.

"The economic performance of the United States is the best in the world, given its high growth rate, stable prices and rising demand for employment," said Noriyuki Mizukami, head of Treasury sales at National Westminster Bank.
Analysts also said that Japan's fledgling economic growth and upcoming election mean no rise in domestic rates is expected.
"The current trend is apparently one of selling currencies with low interest rates in favour of high-yielders," Mizukami said.
The dollar climbed from the opening of trade, hitting 111.00 yen in the early morning for the first time since July 8.
Many Tokyo dealers said the dollar's rise to 113 yen is likely within a month and some predicted it could hit 115 yen.
The dollar has been rising almost steadily since tumbling to a post-war low of 79.75 yen in April 1995.

The yen had been continuously pushed up by U.S. and Japanese central banks as part of a drive to cut Japan's trade surplus, which is now on a downward trend and less of a political issue between the two countries.
The G7 meeting also pushed yields on Japanese government bonds lower with the bellwether 182nd Japanese government bond falling to 2.805 percent from Friday's 2.870 percent.

"The yield for the key cash JGB may fall as low as 2.6 percent during the year. The supply and demand balance will continue to stay fundamentally sound, which will support the JGB," said Hidenobu Furuhashi, manager at Toyo Trust.
That in turn is expected to send yield-deprived Japanese investors into foreign assets, increasing the demand for dollars.

Japan's swelling public debt, accounting for about 90 percent of its gross domestic product, may become another yen selling factor, he added. Japan now has the largest public debt load of any major industrialised nation.
